Spotted archerfish (Toxotes chatareus) eggs, which are demersal and adhesive, hatch after a brief incubation period of approximately 6 days [ab = approximately 6 days] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. The newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, with an initial wet weight at birth of just 0.00005 grams [Wwb = 0.00005 grams], a mass that corresponds closely to the egg diameter of 0.46 millimeters typical for this species. These lecithotrophic larvae rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-eclosion, absorbing nutrients progressively until the mouth opens and the onset of exogenous feeding begins. The brevity of this embryonic period, lasting less than a week under these controlled thermal conditions, is a common trait among tropical teleosts that spawn in warm, shallow waters where rapid development reduces the vulnerability of incubating eggs to predation and environmental fluctuation.

Juvenile Toxotes chatareus experience a prolonged period of somatic growth before reaching reproductive maturity. The total length at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal activity, is estimated at approximately 10.6 centimeters [Lp = approximately 10.6 centimeters], a size that individuals typically attain after about one and a half years of growth. The time since birth at which puberty occurs has been recorded at approximately 547.5 days [tp = approximately 547.5 days] under the same thermal regime of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], reflecting a relatively slow maturation schedule for a fish of this body plan. At the point of sexual maturation, individuals have a corresponding wet weight at puberty of approximately 20 grams [Wwp = approximately 20 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships that indicate a robust, fusiform body shape. This transition to maturity is accompanied by the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, initiating vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males, preparing the fish for their first spawning event.

As adults, Spotted archerfish attain a maximum recorded size, with the ultimate total length reaching up to 40 centimeters [Li = up to 40 centimeters] in the wild. The corresponding ultimate wet weight at this asymptotic size is approximately 1062 grams [Wwi = approximately 1062 grams], representing a substantial increase from the juvenile phase. These measurements, drawn from field surveys of mature individuals, place Toxotes chatareus among the larger members of its genus. The length-weight relationship underlying this mass estimate follows a cubic allometric scaling typical of most bony fishes, where mass increases roughly as the cube of length. At this maximum size, individuals are capable of delivering a powerful jet of water to dislodge terrestrial prey from overhanging vegetation, a feeding strategy that requires both precise neuromuscular coordination and a well-developed buccal cavity. The energy demands of maintaining this body mass are met through a diet consisting primarily of insects and other arthropods, supplemented by small fishes.

The lifespan of Spotted archerfish is relatively extended for a tropical freshwater teleost, with maximum recorded longevity reaching approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] at a water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This relatively slow pace of life, characterized by a late maturation and a moderate lifespan, contrasts with many small-bodied cypriniforms that complete their life cycles in one or two years. Senescence in older individuals is marked by a gradual decline in feeding efficiency and reproductive output, with fewer gravid females observed among the oldest age classes during the spawning season. Field records indicate that natural mortality increases sharply after the fourth year, with very few individuals surviving beyond the fifth year. This pattern of age-related death is consistent with an iteroparous reproductive strategy, where adults invest in multiple spawning events across several seasons, rather than a single, catastrophic reproductive effort. The stable thermal environment of 27.9 °C likely contributes to the consistent metabolic rates and growth trajectories observed throughout adult life.

Comparative analyses within the family Toxotidae reveal that Toxotes chatareus displays a length at puberty of 10.6 centimeters [Lp = 10.6 centimeters] that is intermediate among congeners, with some smaller species maturing at a slightly shorter body length. The size at first reproduction is primarily constrained by the need to achieve a sufficient gape to capture large terrestrial arthropods, a foraging specialization that sets archerfish apart from most other surface-feeding fish. Studying the life-history trade-offs in this species provides insight into how a specialized hunting mode influences the timing of maturation and overall reproductive output. Field observations of spawning aggregations suggest that individuals may delay first reproduction by several months beyond the onset of gonadal maturity, likely waiting for optimal hydrological conditions or prey availability. Continued monitoring of wild populations is essential to understand how environmental variability, particularly fluctuations in water temperature around the optimum of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C], might alter the timing of these critical life-history events.
